title: Greetings come in pairs
summary: Most Arabic greetings have a fixed reply. Learn them as pairs.
explanation: When someone says السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ (peace be upon you), the reply is وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ (and upon you be peace). صَبَاحُ الْخَيْر (morning of goodness) is answered with صَبَاحُ النُّور (morning of light). مَرْحَبًا (hello) is often answered with مَرْحَبًا or أَهْلًا. These are fixed phrases: say them exactly, even if you don't analyse every word yet.

title: I, you, he, she
summary: Arabic has a different word for 'you' when you speak to a man and to a woman.
formula: أَنَا I · أَنْتَ you (m) · أَنْتِ you (f) · هُوَ he · هِيَ she
explanation: The words look almost the same on paper: only the last vowel changes. أَنْتَ (anta) is for a man, أَنْتِ (anti) for a woman. Without harakat both are written أنت, so the vowel marks matter while you learn.

title: my, your: endings on the noun
summary: 'My' and 'your' are endings joined to the end of the noun.
formula: noun + ـِي (my) · ـُكَ (your, m) · ـُكِ (your, f)
explanation: اِسْم means 'name'. Add ـِي to get اِسْمِي (my name). Add ـُكَ when you talk to a man (اِسْمُكَ, your name) and ـُكِ when you talk to a woman (اِسْمُكِ). The ending is written joined to the word: never as a separate word.

examples.en: What is your name? (to a man)

title: No word for 'am / is / are'
summary: In the present tense, Arabic puts two words side by side without a verb 'to be'.
formula: subject + description  (أَنَا + مِصْرِيّ = I am Egyptian)
explanation: أَنَا مِصْرِيّ is literally 'I Egyptian'. The 'am' is understood. This kind of sentence, which starts with a noun or pronoun, is called a nominal sentence. Questions work the same way: أَيْنَ الْبَيْت؟ 'where (is) the house?'.

title: Nationality words: -ī and -iyya
summary: Add ـِيّ to a country to say a man's nationality, and ـِيَّة for a woman's.
explanation: مِصْر (Egypt) → مِصْرِيّ (an Egyptian man) → مِصْرِيَّة (an Egyptian woman). Drop a final ā or the article first: لُبْنَان → لُبْنَانِيّ. The feminine adds ة, which you will meet on every feminine word.

title: Question words
summary: Question words go at the start of the sentence.
formula: question word + rest of the sentence + ؟
explanation: كَيْفَ (how), أَيْنَ (where), مَا (what, before a noun) and مَنْ (who) start the question. The Arabic question mark ؟ is a mirrored ?. For yes/no questions, put هَلْ at the start: هَلْ أَنْتَ مِصْرِيّ؟ (Are you Egyptian?).

title: this: هٰذَا and هٰذِهِ (gender)
summary: Every noun is masculine or feminine. Use هٰذَا for masculine and هٰذِهِ for feminine.
formula: هٰذَا + masculine noun · هٰذِهِ + feminine noun
explanation: Most feminine nouns end in ة (a tied t): عَائِلَة, سَيَّارَة. Female people are feminine too, with or without ة: أُمّ (mother), بِنْت (girl). Note the small upright alif in هٰذَا and هٰذِهِ: it is a long ā that is not written as a full letter.

title: the: الـ (al-)
summary: 'The' is الـ joined to the front of the noun. There is no word for 'a'.
formula: الـ + noun  (كِتَاب a book → الْكِتَاب the book)
explanation: A noun without الـ means 'a': كِتَاب = a book. With الـ it means 'the'. Before a sun letter the l is not said and the next letter is doubled (السَّيَّارَة as-sayyāra). Before a moon letter the l is said (الْقَلَم al-qalam).

title: Adjectives follow and agree
summary: An adjective comes after its noun and matches it in gender and in 'the'.
formula: noun + adjective (same gender, both with or both without الـ)
explanation: كِتَاب جَدِيد = a new book. سَيَّارَة جَدِيدَة = a new car (feminine adds ة to the adjective). الْكِتَاب الْجَدِيد = the new book. But الْكِتَاب جَدِيد (only the noun has الـ) is a sentence: the book is new.

title: Numbers 1–10
summary: Learn the counting forms 1–10 and the Arabic digits ١ to ١٠.
explanation: These are the forms used when counting and in phone numbers. Arabic digits are written left to right inside right-to-left text: ١٢ is twelve. With nouns, 3–10 have special rules that come later in the course.

examples.en: My number is five seven three.

title: Jobs for men and women
summary: A job word for a woman usually adds ة to the word for a man.
explanation: طَالِب is a male student and طَالِبَة a female student. Almost every job works the same way: مُهَنْدِس → مُهَنْدِسَة, طَبِيب → طَبِيبَة. Use the form that matches the person: هِيَ طَبِيبَة (she is a doctor). There is no word for 'a': أَنَا مُمَرِّض means 'I am a nurse'. To ask about a job, say مَا عَمَلُكَ؟ to a man and مَا عَمَلُكِ؟ to a woman.

title: Noun + noun: 'the … of …' (iḍāfa)
summary: Put two nouns side by side to say 'the X of Y': يَوْمُ الْجُمُعَة, Friday (literally 'the day of Friday').
formula: noun (no الـ) + noun with الـ, a name or a 'my/your' ending
explanation: In كِتَابُ دَانْيَال (Daniel's book) the first noun never takes الـ, yet it is definite: 'the book of Daniel'. The second noun is a name, a noun with الـ, or a noun with an ending such as ـِي. A ة at the end of the first noun is said as t: مَدْرَسَةُ اللُّغَة (madrasatu l-lugha, the language school). In careful speech the first noun carries a case vowel (often -u) and the second takes -i; at the end of a sentence the last vowel is usually dropped.

title: Telling the time
summary: Say السَّاعَة (the hour) and a feminine ordinal: السَّاعَة الثَّالِثَة, three o'clock.
formula: السَّاعَة + ordinal (f) + وَالرُّبْع / وَالنِّصْف / إِلَّا رُبْعًا
explanation: Ask كَمِ السَّاعَة؟ (what time is it?, literally 'how much is the hour?'). Answer with السَّاعَة and the feminine 'first, second, third…' word, because سَاعَة is feminine: السَّاعَة الْخَامِسَة (five o'clock). One o'clock is السَّاعَة الْوَاحِدَة. Add وَالرُّبْع (and a quarter), وَالنِّصْف (and a half) or إِلَّا رُبْعًا (minus a quarter). Add صَبَاحًا for the morning and مَسَاءً for the evening. 'At' a time is فِي: فِي السَّاعَة التَّاسِعَة (at nine o'clock).

title: The present tense: I, you, he, she
summary: A present-tense verb adds a prefix for the person: a- for I, ta- for you, ya- for he.
formula: a- (I) · ta- (you, m) · ta- … -īna (you, f) · ya- (he) · ta- (she) + stem + -u
explanation: Arabic verbs change at the front to show who is doing the action. Take ذَهَبَ (he went): أَذْهَبُ (I go), تَذْهَبُ (you go, to a man), تَذْهَبِينَ (you go, to a woman), يَذْهَبُ (he goes), تَذْهَبُ (she goes). 'You' (m) and 'she' look the same; the pronoun or the context tells them apart. The pronoun is usually left out, because the verb already shows the person: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَة means 'I go to school'. One present form covers 'I go', 'I am going' and 'I do go'.

title: We, you all, they: plural verbs
summary: With 'we' the prefix is na-; with 'you' (a group) and 'they' the verb also ends in -ūna.
formula: نَحْنُ نَدْرُسُ · أَنْتُمْ تَدْرُسُونَ · هُمْ يَدْرُسُونَ
explanation: You already know أَدْرُسُ (I study) and يَدْرُسُ (he studies). For 'we', the prefix is na-: نَدْرُسُ (we study). For 'you' talking to a group, and for 'they', the verb takes a prefix and the ending ـُونَ: أَنْتُمْ تَدْرُسُونَ (you study), هُمْ يَدْرُسُونَ (they study). أَنْتُمْ and هُمْ are used for groups of men and for mixed groups.

title: Not: لَا before a present verb
summary: Put لَا before a present-tense verb to say 'not': لَا أَعْرِفُ, I don't know.
explanation: On its own لَا means 'no'. Before a present-tense verb it means 'not', and the verb itself does not change: أَفْهَمُ (I understand) → لَا أَفْهَمُ (I don't understand); يَعْمَلُ (he works) → لَا يَعْمَلُ (he doesn't work). English needs 'do' or 'does'; Arabic does not. لَا is only for verbs: to say 'I am not …' in a sentence without a verb, Arabic uses لَيْسَ, which comes in week 5.

title: Colours: masculine and feminine
summary: The basic colours have a masculine form like أَحْمَر and a feminine form like حَمْرَاء.
explanation: The basic colours share one pattern. The masculine starts with أَ: أَحْمَر (red), أَزْرَق (blue). The feminine has a different shape ending in ـَاء: حَمْرَاء, زَرْقَاء. Like every adjective, a colour comes after its noun and matches it: قَلَم أَحْمَر (a red pen), سَيَّارَة حَمْرَاء (a red car). Some colours come from things and work like nationality words, with ـِيّ and ـِيَّة: بُنِّيّ, بُنِّيَّة (brown, from coffee beans).
